title: A conversation is not a consequence
author: Shaun Brien
summary: Australian teacher Shaun Brien defends a national behaviour curriculum in response to a Centre for Independent Studies report by Blaise Joseph and to critics such as restorative practice advocate Adam Voigt. He opens by rejecting the labelling of explicit teaching and science of learning advocates as right wing, casting their concern as equity for the most vulnerable students. Brien highlights the report's estimate that nine of every thirty minutes of class time are lost to disruption, about twelve weeks a year, and its finding that one in ten teachers report harm to their wellbeing. He argues that consistent, non-negotiable expectations reduce students' micro-decisions and free attention for learning, while class-by-class co-authored codes of conduct leave vague, shifting rules. Pointing to declining student wellbeing across systems with very different pedagogies and to Michaela Community School's results, he concludes that consistent consequences are preventative rather than punitive.
points: The cited survey estimates that 30 percent of class time is lost to disruption, which Brien translates into a full teaching year lost every four years.
He distinguishes suspension from rehabilitation: a restorative conversation can accompany a suspension, but the suspension itself is a punishment.
Student wellbeing declined similarly in England, Scotland and Wales despite divergent teaching approaches, so it cannot be blamed on one method.
Consistent routines work as cognitive offloading, removing micro-decisions so attention goes to learning.
Brien rejects co-authored class codes of conduct because novices lack the expertise to set the conditions for their own learning.
quotes: For the TL:DR (too long, didn’t read), Blaise found that on average 9 minutes out of every 30 minutes of class time were lost to disruption. Equating to around 12 weeks of lost learning time per year.
These suspensions will actually go alongside a restorative conversation which aims to address the root cause of the behaviour, but in reality a suspension is a punishment, it is not rehabilitation.
I just do not understand the argument against having a series of standards of behaviour which we determine to be non-negotiables for the majority of classrooms.
But why are we having young students who do not actually know what is best for learning make decisions about the environment which they are supposed to be learning within?

The whole idea of consistency and routine is that we are helping students with cognitive offloading. We are removing the micro-decisions which students need to make all throughout the day so that their attention can be optimised towards the learning which matters.
That’s not to say that it has never had a negative impact on a single student, but in education we do not work in what works for one student. We work in what benefits the most students possible.
Consistent expectations and consequences around behaviour are not punitive, they are preventative tools which support our teachers to do the important job of teaching.
